services.name: Oral submucous fibrosis (OSMF)
services.description: Oral Submucous Fibrosis, commonly known as OSMF, is a condition in which the inner lining of the mouth gradually becomes stiff due to fibrosis. Because of this stiffness, the patient may find it difficult to open the mouth properly, chew food, speak comfortably, or maintain oral hygiene.OSMF is commonly associated with habits such as paan, gutkha, betel nut/supari chewing, smokeless tobacco, smoking, and alcohol consumption. Early diagnosis and stopping these habits are very important to prevent further progression.In such cases we do fibrotomy to rele all shrink muscles and if nneds we remove them snd replaces with buccal fat-pador nasolabial flap depends upon severity of the case.

content_blocks.heading: Overview

expertise.overview: Head and neck cancers include cancers of the oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and salivary glands. These cancers are among the most common in India, often linked to tobacco and alcohol use. Early detection and surgical intervention by a specialist head and neck oncosurgeon can significantly improve outcomes.
keyPoints: Includes oral, pharyngeal, laryngeal, sinonasal, and salivary gland cancers
Tobacco, alcohol, and HPV are major risk factors
Surgery is the primary treatment for most head and neck cancers
Multidisciplinary approach with radiation and chemotherapy when needed
Early-stage cancers have cure rates above 80%
Reconstruction surgery restores form and function after tumor removal
whenToConsult: Non-healing ulcer or sore in the mouth lasting more than 2-3 weeks
Persistent lump or swelling in the neck
Difficulty swallowing or change in voice lasting more than 2 weeks
Unexplained bleeding from mouth, nose, or throat
White or red patches inside the mouth
treatment: Surgical excision of tumor with adequate margins
Neck dissection for lymph node involvement

faqs.question: What are the early signs of head and neck cancer?
faqs.answer: Non-healing mouth ulcer, persistent lump in neck, difficulty swallowing, voice change, or unexplained bleeding from mouth or nose lasting more than 2-3 weeks.

faqs.question: Is head and neck cancer curable?
faqs.answer: Yes, when detected early, cure rates are above 80%. Even advanced cases can be effectively treated with surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy.

faqs.question: What causes head and neck cancer?
faqs.answer: Tobacco (chewing and smoking), alcohol, betel nut use, HPV infection, and chronic irritation are the most common causes.

expertise.overview: Accurate diagnosis of head and neck cancers involves clinical examination, imaging studies, and tissue biopsy. Early diagnosis is critical for better treatment outcomes and preserving function.
keyPoints: Clinical examination of oral cavity, neck, and throat
Biopsy (incisional or punch) confirms cancer type and grade
CT scan and MRI for tumor extent and staging
PET-CT for detecting distant metastasis
Fine needle aspiration (FNAC) for neck lumps
TNM staging guides treatment planning
whenToConsult: Any lump or swelling in the neck persisting more than 2 weeks
Non-healing mouth ulcer or growth
Unexplained weight loss with throat symptoms
Difficulty opening the mouth (trismus)
Numbness or tingling in face or tongue
treatment: Imaging: CT, MRI, PET-CT as needed

faqs.question: How is head and neck cancer diagnosed?
faqs.answer: Through clinical examination, biopsy of the lesion, imaging (CT/MRI/PET-CT), and FNAC of neck lumps. Biopsy is the gold standard for confirmation.

faqs.question: Is biopsy painful?
faqs.answer: Biopsy is done under local anesthesia and causes minimal discomfort. Results are typically available within 3-5 days.

faqs.question: What scans are needed for cancer staging?
faqs.answer: CT scan of head, neck and chest, MRI for soft tissue detail, and PET-CT for detecting distant spread are commonly used.

expertise.overview: Treatment of head and neck cancer depends on the site, stage, and patient factors. Options include surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy. A multimodality approach is often needed for advanced cancers.
keyPoints: Surgery is the mainstay for resectable tumors
Radiation therapy as primary treatment or post-operative adjuvant
Chemotherapy combined with radiation for advanced stages
Immunotherapy for recurrent or metastatic cancers
Targeted therapy for specific molecular profiles
Rehabilitation includes speech therapy and swallowing therapy
whenToConsult: After confirmed diagnosis of head and neck cancer
For second opinion on treatment plan
When current treatment is not showing response
For reconstruction planning after cancer surgery
For voice rehabilitation after laryngectomy

faqs.question: What is the best treatment for head and neck cancer?
faqs.answer: Treatment depends on cancer type, stage, and location. Surgery is preferred for resectable tumors, with radiation/chemotherapy as adjuvant or for non-surgical candidates.

faqs.question: Does radiation therapy have side effects?
faqs.answer: Common side effects include dry mouth, difficulty swallowing, taste changes, and skin irritation. Most improve after treatment completion.

faqs.question: Can cancer be treated without surgery?
faqs.answer: Early laryngeal and some oropharyngeal cancers can be treated with radiation alone. However, surgery offers best results for most oral cancers.

expertise.summary: Cancer spreads (metastasizes) through direct extension into adjacent tissues, lymphatic spread to regional lymph nodes, ...

content_blocks.heading: Overview
content_blocks.body: See detailed content in expertise detail page.

expertise.overview: Cancer spreads (metastasizes) through direct extension into adjacent tissues, lymphatic spread to regional lymph nodes, and hematogenous (blood) spread to distant organs. Understanding spread patterns helps in staging and treatment planning.
keyPoints: Direct extension: tumor grows into adjacent structures
Lymphatic spread: cancer cells travel to lymph nodes in the neck
Hematogenous spread: cancer reaches lungs, bones, liver through blood
Perineural invasion: cancer spreads along nerve pathways
Staging (TNM) assesses the extent of spread
Early detection prevents metastatic disease
whenToConsult: When diagnosed with any cancer for staging workup
New lump in neck after cancer treatment
Persistent pain in bones or unexplained weight loss
Follow-up surveillance after cancer treatment
Before starting any cancer treatment for complete staging
treatment: Complete surgical removal with clear margins
Neck dissection for lymph node metastasis

faqs.question: How does oral cancer spread?
faqs.answer: Oral cancer spreads first to nearby lymph nodes in the neck, then can spread to lungs, bones, and liver through blood. Local spread to adjacent tissues also occurs.

faqs.question: Can cancer spread be prevented?
faqs.answer: Early detection and complete surgical removal with clear margins is the best way to prevent spread. Regular follow-up detects recurrence early.

faqs.question: What is staging in cancer?
faqs.answer: Staging (TNM system) assesses tumor size (T), lymph node involvement (N), and distant metastasis (M) to determine cancer extent and guide treatment.

content_blocks.heading: Overview

expertise.overview: Oral precancerous lesions include leukoplakia, erythroplakia, and oral submucous fibrosis (OSMF). These conditions have potential to transform into oral cancer if left untreated. Early intervention can prevent malignant transformation.
keyPoints: Leukoplakia: white patches that cannot be wiped off
Erythroplakia: red patches with higher malignant potential
Oral submucous fibrosis: progressive fibrosis causing restricted mouth opening
Tobacco and betel nut are primary causes
Malignant transformation rate varies from 1% to 50% depending on type
Regular biopsy and follow-up is essential
whenToConsult: White or red patch inside mouth lasting more than 2 weeks
Difficulty opening the mouth fully
Burning sensation while eating spicy food
Any change in size, color, or texture of existing patch
Tobacco users with any oral symptoms
treatment: Medical management with antioxidants and supplements
Surgical release of fibrosis bands in OSMF
Regular follow-up with biopsy if changes occur

faqs.question: Can leukoplakia turn into cancer?
faqs.answer: Yes, leukoplakia has 1-20% malignant transformation rate. Erythroplakia has even higher risk (up to 50%). Regular monitoring and biopsy are essential.

faqs.question: How is oral submucous fibrosis treated?
faqs.answer: Treatment includes strict cessation of betel nut/tobacco, medications, physiotherapy for mouth opening, and surgical release of fibrotic bands in severe cases.

faqs.question: Should I get a biopsy for a white patch in my mouth?
faqs.answer: Yes, any white or red patch lasting more than 2 weeks should be evaluated. Biopsy helps determine if it is precancerous and guides treatment.

expertise.overview: India has one of the highest rates of oral cancer globally, accounting for nearly one-third of all cancers in the country. Tobacco chewing, betel nut, smoking, and alcohol are major risk factors unique to the Indian population.
keyPoints: India accounts for 30% of global oral cancer cases
Most common cancer in Indian males
Average age of presentation is 40-50 years
Tobacco chewing (gutka, khaini, paan) is the leading cause
Late presentation is common due to lack of awareness
Early detection through screening can save lives
whenToConsult: Any non-healing ulcer in the mouth
Difficulty in chewing or swallowing
Loosening of teeth without dental cause
Swelling or lump on jaw or neck
Change in voice or persistent sore throat
treatment: Surgery for early and locally advanced cancers
Radiation and chemotherapy for advanced stages
Public awareness and tobacco cessation programs

faqs.question: Why is oral cancer so common in India?
faqs.answer: High prevalence of tobacco chewing (gutka, paan, khaini), betel nut use, smoking, and alcohol consumption. Late presentation due to lack of awareness also contributes.

faqs.question: At what age does oral cancer occur?
faqs.answer: In India, oral cancer commonly presents between 40-50 years, but increasingly seen in younger patients (30-40 years) due to gutka and tobacco use.

faqs.question: Can oral cancer be prevented?
faqs.answer: Yes, by avoiding tobacco in all forms, limiting alcohol, maintaining good oral hygiene, and getting regular dental check-ups. Early detection through screening saves lives.

expertise.overview: Oral cancer affects the lips, tongue, cheeks, floor of mouth, hard palate, and gums. It is one of the most common cancers in India. With early diagnosis and expert surgical treatment, cure rates are high.
keyPoints: Tongue cancer is the most common subsite
Buccal mucosa (cheek) cancer is common in tobacco chewers
TNM staging determines treatment approach
Surgery with clear margins is the gold standard
Reconstruction preserves speech and swallowing
5-year survival rate for early-stage is above 70%
whenToConsult: Non-healing ulcer or growth in the mouth
Pain while chewing or swallowing
Numbness of lip, chin, or tongue
Bleeding from the mouth
Lump or thickening in cheek or neck
treatment: Partial or total glossectomy for tongue cancers

faqs.question: What are the types of oral cancer?
faqs.answer: Oral cancer includes tongue cancer, buccal mucosa (cheek) cancer, lip cancer, floor of mouth cancer, gum cancer, and hard palate cancer. Tongue is the most common site.

faqs.question: What is the survival rate of oral cancer?
faqs.answer: Early-stage oral cancer has 70-90% five-year survival rate. Advanced stages have 30-50% survival. Early detection is crucial for better outcomes.

faqs.question: How is oral cancer surgery performed?
faqs.answer: Tumor is removed with adequate margins, neck dissection is done if needed, and reconstruction with flaps restores form and function for eating and speaking.

expertise.overview: Human Papillomavirus (HPV), particularly HPV-16, is an emerging risk factor for oropharyngeal cancers (tonsil and base of tongue). HPV-related cancers tend to occur in younger patients and generally have better prognosis than tobacco-related cancers.
keyPoints: HPV-16 is the most common type associated with oropharyngeal cancer
Affects tonsil and base of tongue primarily
Often presents as neck lump in younger patients
Better response to treatment compared to HPV-negative cancers
HPV vaccination can prevent these cancers
p16 immunohistochemistry is used for detection
whenToConsult: Persistent sore throat lasting more than 3 weeks
Painless neck lump in a young adult
Difficulty swallowing or ear pain on one side
Unexplained weight loss with throat symptoms
For HPV vaccination counseling
treatment: Surgery (transoral robotic surgery) for early stages
Radiation therapy with or without chemotherapy
De-escalation protocols being studied for HPV-positive cancers

faqs.question: Can HPV cause mouth cancer?
faqs.answer: Yes, HPV-16 causes oropharyngeal cancer (tonsil and base of tongue). It accounts for 25-30% of oropharyngeal cancers and is increasing in prevalence.

faqs.question: Does HPV vaccination prevent oral cancer?
faqs.answer: Yes, HPV vaccination (given before age 26) significantly reduces the risk of HPV-related oropharyngeal cancers.

faqs.question: Is HPV-related cancer different from tobacco-related cancer?
faqs.answer: Yes, HPV-related cancers typically occur in younger patients, have better prognosis, and respond better to treatment compared to tobacco-related cancers.

expertise.overview: Reconstruction after head and neck cancer surgery aims to restore form and function. Modern microvascular free flap techniques allow reconstruction of complex defects, enabling patients to eat, speak, and live with dignity after cancer treatment.
keyPoints: Microvascular free flaps are the gold standard
Radial forearm flap for tongue and floor of mouth
Fibula flap for jaw (mandible) reconstruction
ALT flap for large soft tissue defects
Pectoralis major flap as a workhorse pedicled flap
Goal: restore speech, swallowing, and cosmesis
whenToConsult: After diagnosis when surgery will create a large defect
For jaw reconstruction planning
When previous surgery left functional deficit
For cosmetic improvement after cancer treatment
Speech or swallowing difficulty after surgery
treatment: Bone reconstruction with fibula or scapula flap

faqs.question: Will I look normal after cancer surgery?
faqs.answer: Modern reconstruction techniques using microvascular free flaps restore facial appearance significantly. The goal is to maintain both function and cosmesis.

faqs.question: Can I eat and speak normally after jaw reconstruction?
faqs.answer: Yes, fibula flap reconstruction of the jaw followed by dental implants allows near-normal eating. Speech therapy helps regain clear speech.

faqs.question: What is a free flap surgery?
faqs.answer: A free flap involves transferring tissue (skin, muscle, bone) from another body part with its blood vessels, reconnected under microscope at the defect site.

content_blocks.heading: Overview
content_blocks.body: Diagnosis and surgical management of salivary gland tumors.

expertise.overview: Salivary gland tumors can arise in the parotid, submandibular, or minor salivary glands. Most parotid tumors are benign (pleomorphic adenoma), but malignant tumors require complete surgical excision with careful preservation of the facial nerve.
keyPoints: Parotid gland tumors are the most common
80% of parotid tumors are benign
Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common benign tumor
Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the most common malignant tumor
FNAC helps in preoperative diagnosis
Facial nerve preservation is critical during surgery
whenToConsult: Painless swelling near ear or under jaw
Rapidly growing lump in front of ear
Facial weakness or numbness with a salivary gland lump
Pain or fixity of a salivary gland mass
Recurrent salivary gland swelling
treatment: Total parotidectomy with nerve preservation for malignant tumors
Neck dissection if lymph nodes involved

faqs.question: Is a lump near the ear always cancer?
faqs.answer: No, 80% of parotid tumors are benign. However, any persistent lump should be evaluated with FNAC and imaging to rule out malignancy.

faqs.question: What happens if salivary gland tumor is not treated?
faqs.answer: Benign tumors can grow large and rarely transform to cancer (carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma). Malignant tumors can spread to neck nodes and beyond.

faqs.question: Will my face be affected after parotid surgery?
faqs.answer: Expert surgeons preserve the facial nerve during parotid surgery. Temporary weakness may occur but permanent damage is rare with experienced surgeons.

content_blocks.body: Specialized surgical techniques for parotid gland tumors with nerve preservation.

expertise.overview: Parotid surgery involves removal of tumors from the parotid gland while preserving the facial nerve that runs through it. Expert surgical technique is essential to avoid facial paralysis and ensure complete tumor removal.
keyPoints: Facial nerve identification and preservation is paramount
Superficial parotidectomy for tumors in superficial lobe
Total parotidectomy for deep lobe tumors
Nerve monitoring may be used during surgery
Risk of Frey syndrome (gustatory sweating) post-surgery
Minimal scarring with modified Blair incision
whenToConsult: Lump in front of or below the ear
Growing swelling in the parotid region
Facial weakness associated with parotid swelling
Recurrent parotid tumor after previous surgery
Pain or rapid growth of existing lump
treatment: Total parotidectomy for deep lobe tumors
Nerve grafting if sacrifice is necessary

faqs.question: Is parotid surgery safe?
faqs.answer: Yes, with an experienced head and neck surgeon. The key risk is facial nerve injury, which is minimized with expert technique and nerve monitoring.

faqs.question: How long is recovery after parotid surgery?
faqs.answer: Most patients go home in 2-3 days. Swelling resolves in 2-3 weeks. Full recovery takes 4-6 weeks. Facial nerve function recovers within weeks if temporarily affected.

faqs.question: Will there be a visible scar?
faqs.answer: The incision is placed in a natural skin crease (modified Blair incision) in front of the ear, making it minimally visible after healing.

content_blocks.body: Understanding cancer fundamentals and early warning signs.

expertise.overview: Cancer is the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in the body. In oral cancer, cells in the mouth or throat grow out of control, forming tumors that can invade surrounding tissues and spread to other parts of the body.
keyPoints: Cancer occurs when normal cell growth regulation fails
Mutations in DNA cause cells to divide uncontrollably
Benign tumors do not spread; malignant tumors (cancer) can spread
Risk factors include tobacco, alcohol, UV exposure, and genetic predisposition
Early symptoms: non-healing sore, lump, unexplained bleeding
Early detection dramatically improves survival rates
whenToConsult: Any lump or swelling that persists for more than 2 weeks
Non-healing wound or ulcer
Unexplained weight loss
Persistent pain without clear cause
Change in a mole or skin lesion
Difficulty swallowing or breathing

faqs.question: What is the difference between benign and malignant tumors?
faqs.answer: Benign tumors grow slowly, do not spread, and are usually harmless. Malignant tumors (cancer) grow rapidly, invade surrounding tissues, and can spread to distant organs.

faqs.question: Is cancer hereditary?
faqs.answer: Some cancers have genetic component, but most head and neck cancers are caused by environmental factors like tobacco and alcohol rather than heredity.

faqs.question: Can cancer come back after treatment?
faqs.answer: Yes, recurrence is possible. Regular follow-up with clinical examination and imaging for 5 years after treatment helps detect recurrence early.

expertise.title: Why do people who have never used tobacco or alcohol get oral cancer
expertise.summary: While tobacco and alcohol are the most common causes, oral cancer can also occur in people who have never used these sub...

content_blocks.heading: Overview
content_blocks.body: Non-traditional risk factors and emerging causes of oral cancer.

expertise.overview: While tobacco and alcohol are the most common causes, oral cancer can also occur in people who have never used these substances. Other risk factors include HPV infection, genetic predisposition, chronic irritation, nutritional deficiencies, and immune suppression.
keyPoints: HPV infection (especially HPV-16) is an emerging cause
Genetic mutations can predispose to cancer without external risk factors
Chronic dental irritation from sharp teeth or ill-fitting dentures
Nutritional deficiency (iron, vitamin A) may increase risk
Immune suppression (HIV, organ transplant patients)
Betel nut chewing without tobacco is also a risk factor
whenToConsult: Non-healing oral ulcer even without tobacco history
Family history of oral or head and neck cancer
Persistent oral symptoms without obvious cause
HPV-positive diagnosis with oropharyngeal symptoms
Any suspicious oral lesion regardless of habits
treatment: Same treatment principles as tobacco-related cancers
HPV-related cancers may have different protocols

faqs.question: Can non-smokers get oral cancer?
faqs.answer: Yes, though less common. HPV infection, genetic factors, chronic irritation, nutritional deficiencies, and betel nut chewing without tobacco can cause oral cancer.

faqs.question: Does stress cause cancer?
faqs.answer: Stress alone does not directly cause cancer, but chronic stress may weaken the immune system. Maintaining healthy lifestyle and regular check-ups is recommended.

faqs.question: Are young people at risk for oral cancer?
faqs.answer: Yes, increasingly younger patients (25-40 years) are being diagnosed, often due to gutka/tobacco habits started early or HPV-related cancers.

expertise.summary: Thyroid cancer is a common endocrine malignancy that typically presents as a neck lump. Most thyroid cancers (papillary ...

content_blocks.heading: Overview
content_blocks.body: Comprehensive thyroid cancer diagnosis and surgical treatment.

expertise.overview: Thyroid cancer is a common endocrine malignancy that typically presents as a neck lump. Most thyroid cancers (papillary and follicular) have excellent prognosis with appropriate surgery. Expert surgical technique preserves the recurrent laryngeal nerve and parathyroid glands.
keyPoints: Papillary thyroid cancer is the most common type (80%)
Usually presents as a painless thyroid nodule
Ultrasound and FNAC are key diagnostic tools
Surgery (thyroidectomy) is the primary treatment
Radioactive iodine therapy for certain cases post-surgery
Excellent prognosis: 5-year survival above 95% for papillary type
whenToConsult: Neck swelling or lump in the thyroid area
Hoarseness of voice with thyroid nodule
Rapidly growing thyroid nodule
Family history of thyroid cancer or MEN syndrome
Thyroid nodule with suspicious ultrasound features
treatment: Total thyroidectomy for larger or bilateral tumors
Central neck dissection if lymph nodes involved

faqs.question: Is thyroid cancer serious?
faqs.answer: Most thyroid cancers (papillary type) have excellent prognosis with 95%+ five-year survival. However, timely surgery is important to prevent spread.

faqs.question: Will I need lifelong medication after thyroid surgery?
faqs.answer: If total thyroidectomy is done, lifelong thyroid hormone (levothyroxine) replacement is needed. After hemithyroidectomy, the remaining lobe usually maintains function.

faqs.question: How is thyroid cancer detected?
faqs.answer: Through neck ultrasound showing suspicious nodule features, followed by Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology (FNAC) which confirms the diagnosis.

content_blocks.heading: Overview
content_blocks.body: Advanced endoscopic and open surgical approaches for skull base tumors.

expertise.overview: Skull base surgery involves removal of tumors at the junction of the skull and face/neck. These complex procedures require expertise in both open craniofacial approaches and endoscopic techniques. Tumors include sinonasal cancers, esthesioneuroblastoma, and invading head and neck cancers.
keyPoints: Open craniofacial resection for anterior skull base tumors
Endoscopic endonasal approaches for select tumors
Multidisciplinary team with neurosurgeon often required
Sinonasal cancers and esthesioneuroblastoma are common indications
CSF leak prevention and management is critical
Advanced imaging (CT + MRI) for surgical planning
whenToConsult: Nasal obstruction with bloody discharge
Loss of smell or facial pain
Tumor involving the paranasal sinuses extending to skull base
Double vision or eye displacement
Recurrent sinonasal polyps with suspicious features

faqs.question: What tumors need skull base surgery?
faqs.answer: Sinonasal cancers, esthesioneuroblastoma, chordoma, meningioma extending to skull base, and locally advanced cancers invading the skull base.

faqs.question: Is skull base surgery dangerous?
faqs.answer: It is complex but safe in experienced hands. Risks include CSF leak, infection, and cranial nerve damage, which are minimized with expert technique.

faqs.question: Can skull base tumors be removed endoscopically?
faqs.answer: Select tumors can be removed through the nose (endoscopic endonasal approach) without external incisions, offering faster recovery.

Endoscopic-assisted neck dissection

Small oropharyngeal tumor suitable for TORS
Submandibular gland pathology
Patient preference for minimal scarring
Suitable tumor size and location for minimally invasive approach
treatment: Endoscopic thyroidectomy via axillary or retroauricular approach

faqs.question: What is scarless thyroid surgery?
faqs.answer: Endoscopic thyroidectomy through axillary (armpit) or retroauricular (behind ear) approach leaves no visible neck scar while achieving the same oncologic result.

faqs.question: Is robotic surgery available for mouth cancer?
faqs.answer: Yes, Transoral Robotic Surgery (TORS) is used for selected oropharyngeal cancers, offering precise removal through the mouth without external cuts.

faqs.question: Who is a good candidate for minimally invasive surgery?
faqs.answer: Patients with small-to-moderate tumors in accessible locations, good general health, and preference for cosmetic outcome are ideal candidates.

content_blocks.heading: Overview
content_blocks.body: Surgical management of larynx and hypopharynx cancers with voice rehabilitation.

expertise.overview: Laryngeal (voice box) and hypopharyngeal cancers affect speech, breathing, and swallowing. Treatment aims to cure cancer while preserving or rehabilitating voice function. Options range from laser surgery for early cancers to total laryngectomy with voice prosthesis for advanced cases.
keyPoints: Hoarseness is the earliest symptom of laryngeal cancer
Smoking and alcohol are primary risk factors
Early glottic cancers have 90%+ cure rate with radiation or laser
Advanced cancers may require total laryngectomy
Voice rehabilitation with tracheoesophageal prosthesis
Dr. Prashant has patent on novel voice prosthesis device
whenToConsult: Hoarseness lasting more than 3 weeks
Difficulty breathing or noisy breathing
Difficulty swallowing or sensation of lump in throat
Ear pain with voice change
Neck lump with voice or swallowing symptoms
treatment: Laser excision for early laryngeal cancers

faqs.question: Will I lose my voice after larynx cancer treatment?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Early cancers can be cured with laser or radiation preserving voice. Even after total laryngectomy, voice rehabilitation with prosthesis is possible.

faqs.question: What is a voice prosthesis?
faqs.answer: A small valve placed between windpipe and food pipe that allows speech after laryngectomy. Dr. Prashant holds a patent on a novel tracheoesophageal voice prosthesis device.

faqs.question: Can larynx cancer be detected early?
faqs.answer: Yes, any hoarseness lasting more than 3 weeks should be evaluated with laryngoscopy. Early glottic cancers have 90%+ cure rate.

expertise.title: Facial Trauma Accidental Cases
expertise.summary: We provide treatment for facial injuries caused by accidents, including jaw fractures, facial bone fractures, dental injuries, cuts, and soft tissue wounds, with a focus on restoring function, comfort, and facial appearance.
expertise.overview:
Facial trauma includes injuries to the face, jaws, teeth, gums, lips, and surrounding soft tissues caused by road accidents, falls, sports injuries, workplace injuries, or physical impact.

These injuries may involve cuts, swelling, bleeding, broken teeth, jaw fractures, cheekbone fractures, or difficulty in opening and closing the mouth. Early diagnosis and timely treatment are important to restore chewing, speech, facial appearance, and normal jaw function.
keyPoints: Treatment for facial cuts, wounds, and soft tissue injuries
Management of jaw fractures and facial bone fractures
Treatment for broken, loose, or displaced teeth after trauma
Jaw fixation or surgical correction may be required in selected cases
Focus on restoring bite, mouth opening, facial function, and appearance
Early treatment helps reduce complications and improves healing
whenToConsult: Accident or fall causing injury to face, jaw, mouth, or teeth
Bleeding wounds, deep cuts, or swelling on the face
Difficulty in opening or closing the mouth
Pain while chewing or change in bite after injury
Broken, loose, missing, or displaced teeth
Numbness over lips, chin, cheeks, or face after injury
Suspected jaw fracture or facial bone fracture
Persistent facial pain, swelling, or deformity after trauma
treatment: Clinical examination and radiographic evaluation such as X-ray or CBCT if required
Cleaning and suturing of facial or oral wounds
Management of dental injuries such as broken, loose, or displaced teeth
Jaw fracture treatment with fixation when required
Facial bone fracture correction depending on severity
Medication for pain, swelling, and infection control
Follow-up care to monitor healing, bite, mouth opening, and facial function
Referral or hospital-based care for severe emergency trauma cases

faqs.question: Is facial trauma an emergency?
faqs.answer: Severe bleeding, breathing difficulty, loss of consciousness, eye injury, or suspected jaw fracture should be treated as an emergency.

faqs.question: Can jaw fracture happen after an accident?
faqs.answer: Yes, road accidents, falls, sports injuries, or direct impact can cause jaw or facial bone fractures.

faqs.question: How is facial trauma diagnosed?
faqs.answer: Diagnosis is done through clinical examination and imaging such as X-ray or CBCT when required.

faqs.question: Is surgery always required?
faqs.answer: No. Minor injuries may need wound care and medicines, while fractures or severe injuries may require fixation or surgery.

faqs.question: Can broken teeth after an accident be treated?
faqs.answer: Yes. Depending on the injury, dental treatment, stabilization, restoration, or replacement may be advised.

faqs.question: Why is early treatment important?
faqs.answer: Early treatment helps restore bite, mouth opening, chewing, speech, facial appearance, and reduces the risk of complications.

expertise.title: Orthognathic Surgery (For Facial Asymmetry)
expertise.summary: Orthognathic surgery helps correct jaw imbalance, facial asymmetry, and abnormal bite by repositioning the upper jaw, lower jaw, or chin to improve function, occlusion, and facial balance.
expertise.overview:
Orthognathic surgery, also known as corrective jaw surgery, is performed for patients with jaw imbalance, facial asymmetry, or skeletal malocclusion where the upper and lower jaws do not meet properly.

Facial asymmetry may affect facial appearance, smile balance, chewing, speech, and bite alignment. In such cases, surgery is carefully planned to reposition the jaws and improve both function and facial harmony.

Depending on the patient’s condition, procedures such as BSSO, Le Fort I osteotomy, or genioplasty may be advised.
keyPoints: Corrects jaw imbalance and facial asymmetry
Helps improve abnormal bite and occlusion
Improves chewing, speech, smile balance, and facial profile
Treatment is planned with clinical examination and radiographic evaluation
May involve upper jaw, lower jaw, or chin correction
Usually requires detailed planning with dental and facial analysis
Focus on functional correction and natural facial balance
whenToConsult: Uneven or asymmetric facial appearance
Upper and lower teeth do not meet properly
Difficulty in chewing due to jaw mismatch
Prominent or retruded lower jaw
Upper jaw deficiency or forwardly placed jaw
Chin appears too small, large, or deviated
Facial imbalance affecting smile or profile
Long-standing skeletal malocclusion requiring surgical correction
treatment: Radiographic evaluation such as X-ray or CBCT if required
BSSO for lower jaw advancement, setback, or correction
Le Fort I osteotomy for upper jaw advancement or repositioning
Genioplasty for chin reshaping or repositioning
Post-surgical follow-up for healing, bite stability, and jaw function

faqs.question: What is orthognathic surgery?
faqs.answer: Orthognathic surgery is corrective jaw surgery used to correct jaw position, bite problems, and facial imbalance.

faqs.question: Is it done only for appearance?
faqs.answer: No. It is mainly done to improve jaw function, bite alignment, chewing, speech, and facial balance.

faqs.question: Can it correct facial asymmetry?
faqs.answer: Yes. In selected cases, jaw repositioning can help improve facial asymmetry and facial harmony.

faqs.question: Which procedures may be required?
faqs.answer: Depending on the case, BSSO, Le Fort I osteotomy, genioplasty, or a combination of procedures may be advised.

faqs.question: Is planning required before surgery?
faqs.answer: Yes. Detailed clinical examination, bite analysis, facial assessment, and radiographic evaluation are required before treatment.

faqs.question: Is orthodontic treatment needed?
faqs.answer: In many cases, orthodontic treatment may be required before or after surgery to achieve proper bite alignment.
